Family Health

A hard lump near the anus: possible causes and what to do

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Finding a firm lump or new swelling near the anus can be worrying. Many causes are treatable and non-cancerous, but similar-looking problems need different care. Start by checking for urgent symptoms, then arrange an examination rather than guessing from appearance.

What a hard area near the anus can mean

The anus is the opening at the end of the digestive tract. The anal canal connects it to the rectum, and the internal and external sphincter muscles help control the passage of stool. The surrounding area contains sensitive skin, blood vessels, glands and other tissues. A change in any of these can be felt as a lump or an area of firmness.

Swelling, a blood clot, a skin growth or an infection can all create that sensation. Constipation can cause a feeling of fullness without a separate skin lump. Many causes are non-cancerous, but touch or a photograph cannot reliably identify them. A new or changing lump deserves an examination, even when embarrassment makes it tempting to wait.

First, decide whether care is urgent

Get emergency help for bleeding that will not stop, a large amount of blood, or severe pain. Worsening anal pain with fever, spreading redness, pus or feeling very unwell needs prompt same-day assessment. An abscess can be deeper than the visible skin and may not produce an obvious external lump.

A retained object in the rectum also needs urgent medical help. Do not try to pull it out with tools. Severe abdominal pain, vomiting, swelling and inability to pass stool or gas can indicate a bowel obstruction and require emergency assessment. A routine appointment is appropriate for many milder symptoms, but persistent bleeding or a change in bowel habits should not simply be attributed to piles.

1. External haemorrhoids

Haemorrhoidal tissue normally forms part of the anal region. It can become enlarged or symptomatic, producing swelling, itching, discomfort or bleeding. External haemorrhoids are covered by sensitive skin; internal ones start farther inside and may protrude. Pregnancy, straining, constipation and heavy lifting can contribute to symptoms.

A clot in an external haemorrhoid can cause a firm, very tender blue-purple lump. A soft skin tag may remain after the swelling settles. Neither a tag nor a lump automatically explains bleeding, however. An examination is especially useful when the symptoms are new, recurrent, worsening or different from a previously diagnosed problem.

Care for haemorrhoids depends on their type

For confirmed uncomplicated piles, gentle cleaning, a warm bath, a wrapped cold pack and measures to make stools easier to pass may help. A pharmacist can advise about a suitable pain medicine or a short course of symptom-relief cream. Avoid prolonged straining and spending unnecessary time on the toilet. Check medicines with a pharmacist if you are pregnant or have other conditions.

Rubber-band treatment and sclerotherapy are procedures for internal haemorrhoids, not treatments to apply to an external lump. Selected severely painful clotted external haemorrhoids may be removed by a clinician; timing and examination guide that decision. Surgery is sometimes used for substantial or persistent disease. Recurrence depends on the condition and procedure, so one percentage cannot describe everyone’s outlook.

2. Hidradenitis suppurativa near the anus

Hidradenitis suppurativa, often shortened to HS, is an inflammatory skin condition that begins around hair follicles. It can cause deep painful nodules in the groin, buttocks and perianal area as well as elsewhere. Some nodules drain, develop an odour, leave scars or become connected by tunnels under the skin.

HS is not caused by being unclean and is not contagious. Recurrent lumps in skin folds are a reason to seek a dermatology assessment. Other conditions, including Crohn-related perianal disease, can produce similar draining areas, so the diagnosis should not be based on location alone. Findings from a small specialist study should not be used to decide who can or cannot have HS.

HS needs an individual treatment plan

Treatment aims to control inflammation, reduce flare-ups and care for painful or draining skin. Depending on severity, a dermatologist may use a topical antibiotic, oral antibiotics or another medicine. A corticosteroid injection can be appropriate for selected inflamed nodules; it is not a reason to apply steroid products indiscriminately to an undiagnosed anal lump.

Biologic medicines are options for some moderate or severe cases. Adalimumab is one example; other approved options now include secukinumab and bimekizumab for eligible adults in some jurisdictions. Persistent tunnels may need a procedure as well as medication. These treatments require diagnosis, monitoring and discussion of infection risks. Do not squeeze or cut the nodules yourself.

3. A perianal haematoma or clotted external swelling

A small collection of blood or clot beneath the skin at the anal margin may be described as a perianal haematoma; terminology overlaps with external haemorrhoidal thrombosis. The swelling can appear suddenly and feel tense or tender, often with a blue or purple colour. It may follow straining, coughing or lifting, although there may be no clear trigger.

Pain can improve before the lump has completely disappeared. A clinician can advise whether comfort measures are enough or an early procedure would be helpful for severe symptoms. Do not puncture it to release the blood. A very large, rapidly enlarging or unusually painful swelling should be assessed rather than considered a normal-sized clot.

4. Anal warts

Anal warts are caused by particular types of human papillomavirus, or HPV. They can occur around the opening or inside the anal canal and may look like small flesh-coloured bumps or clusters. Some cause itching, mucus or bleeding; others are painless. HPV spreads through intimate skin contact, including sexual contact, rather than being defined simply as an infection spread through body fluids.

A clinician can examine the outside and decide whether the inside also needs checking. Atypical, bleeding, ulcerated or uncertain growths may need a biopsy. Most wart-causing HPV types differ from the high-risk types associated with cancer, but appearances alone do not identify the virus type or exclude another condition.

Wart treatment is chosen for the exact location

Options include prescribed treatments for suitable external warts, freezing with liquid nitrogen, surgical removal or electrosurgery. Liquid nitrogen is applied to freeze the tissue; it is not injected into the wart. Warts inside the anus need specialist management. Treatment removes visible lesions but does not guarantee that no new wart will develop.

Imiquimod or podofilox may be prescribed for selected external lesions. Trichloroacetic or bichloroacetic acid is clinician-applied treatment, not a home remedy. Podophyllin resin is no longer a routinely recommended CDC regimen because safer options exist and serious toxicity can occur. Pregnancy affects which medicines are suitable. Never use an ordinary hand-and-foot wart remover on anal or genital skin.

5. Molluscum contagiosum

Molluscum is a different viral skin infection. It usually causes small, firm, pink, white or skin-coloured bumps with a central dip. They may itch or become inflamed. Spread can occur through skin contact, sexual contact, shared contaminated items such as towels, or moving the virus to another area by scratching or shaving.

Many cases clear over months, although some persist much longer. Lesions around the genitals or anus should be checked because other conditions can look similar and treatment is often advised at these sites. Do not squeeze out the centre or try an internet removal product. A clinician can discuss suitable treatment; imiquimod is not a universal first choice and is not recommended for molluscum in children.

6. Constipation and a feeling of fullness

Constipation can mean hard or lumpy stools, difficult passage, straining, incomplete emptying or fewer bowel movements than usual. Fewer than three movements a week is one possible feature, not the only definition. Stool collecting in the rectum can create pressure or a sense of hardness, but it does not explain every visible lump.

Low fibre or inadequate fluid intake may contribute, but medicines, changes in routine and medical conditions can also matter. Repeated straining may aggravate haemorrhoidal symptoms. Tell a clinician about a persistent change from your usual bowel pattern, especially with bleeding, pain or other new symptoms. Do not assume that everyone needs to pass stool on the same schedule.

Constipation treatment is a sequence, not one prescription

Gradually adding fibre-containing foods, drinking an appropriate amount of fluid and keeping active can help many people. Adjust fluid advice if a clinician has given you a restriction. Allow time for the toilet without prolonged pushing. If a medicine may be contributing, ask about it rather than stopping a prescribed treatment yourself.

A pharmacist or clinician may suggest a suitable laxative, such as an osmotic product, or another approach. Lubiprostone is a prescription option for selected situations when simpler measures are insufficient; it is not the automatic treatment for a new anal lump. Suspected impaction, persistent symptoms or signs of obstruction need medical assessment rather than escalating home laxatives.

7. Anal cancer

Anal cancer is an uncommon cause of a lump, but it is one reason a persistent change should be examined. Possible symptoms include bleeding, pain or pressure, itching, discharge and altered bowel habits. These overlap with more common conditions, and the absence of pain does not rule cancer out.

Persistent high-risk HPV infection is a major risk factor; smoking and weakened immunity also affect risk. A suspicious area is assessed and usually sampled with a biopsy. Treatment depends on the cancer type and stage. For many anal squamous cancers, chemotherapy combined with radiotherapy is the main treatment; surgery has a role in selected early lesions or persistent or recurrent disease.

8. A foreign object in the rectum

An object can become stuck after insertion, or occasionally a swallowed sharp fragment can lodge low in the bowel. Pressure, pain, bleeding or a hard sensation may result. Medical teams see these problems and can assess them without needing you to feel ashamed. Explain what the object is and when it entered, because its shape and material affect safe care.

Do not make repeated attempts with fingers, forceps or other tools, and do not force an object farther inside. Examination and imaging may be needed before removal, especially for a sharp object. A trained clinician may remove it under direct vision with pain relief or anaesthesia; some cases require endoscopy or surgery. The area may need checking for injury afterwards.

Another important possibility: an abscess or fistula

An anal abscess is a pocket of infection, often involving an anal gland. It may cause constant or worsening pain, swelling, redness, fever or feeling unwell. Deep abscesses can cause pressure and pain even without a visible bump. They generally need prompt drainage; antibiotics alone are usually not an adequate substitute.

A fistula is a tract that can remain between the anal canal and skin after an abscess. Repeated swelling and drainage from a small opening can be a clue. A colorectal specialist assesses the tract and its relationship to the sphincter muscles before treatment. Crohn-related fistulas may need combined medical and surgical care.

A painless lump still needs the right explanation

Warts, molluscum, skin tags and some haemorrhoidal swellings can be painless. A lack of pain may make an appointment less urgent when you otherwise feel well, but it does not prove a lump is harmless. New growth, persistent bleeding, an ulcer or a change in the surface deserves review.

Avoid repeatedly squeezing the area to test how hard it feels. Instead, note when you first noticed it, whether it is changing, and any discharge, bleeding or bowel symptoms. Bring information about previous anal problems, medicines and relevant health conditions. These details help the clinician decide what needs examination or testing.

How clinicians work out the cause

The first steps usually include a symptom history and inspection of the skin. With your consent, a clinician may perform a gentle gloved-finger rectal examination. An anoscope is a short instrument used to look inside the anal canal. The examination can be adjusted if pain is severe, and you can ask for an explanation and a chaperone.

Depending on what is found, the next step might be a swab, biopsy, specialist assessment or imaging. Further bowel investigation is selected for the symptoms and risk factors, not required for every lump. Flexible sigmoidoscopy examines the lower bowel; colonoscopy looks farther through the colon. A barium enema is an older X-ray examination and is now used less often than alternatives.

Make a follow-up plan after the first visit

Ask what the working diagnosis is, which treatment is intended for it, how soon improvement is expected and when to return if the lump remains. Different conditions can coexist, so treatment for constipation does not necessarily explain a skin lesion, and a familiar haemorrhoid should not automatically account for every new episode of bleeding.

Many causes can be managed successfully, but the useful reassurance comes from an appropriate assessment. Seek earlier help if pain increases, fever appears, bleeding continues or bowel symptoms change. If you are unsure where to start, primary care can arrange assessment and referral to colorectal, dermatology or sexual-health services as needed.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

A new anal lump needs an explanation; pain, colour and firmness alone do not make a diagnosis.

Treatment differs for external clots, internal haemorrhoids, skin infections, inflammatory disease and cancer.

How BeMama can help

Make it easier to seek care by writing down symptoms and asking for privacy, an explanation of the examination and a chaperone if wanted.

When to seek help

Heavy bleeding, severe pain, a retained object, or worsening pain with fever requires urgent medical care. Do not puncture a lump or apply wart-removal acids yourself.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The eight original causes are covered individually, with abscess and fistula added as important alternatives.
  • Internal haemorrhoid procedures should not be applied to external lumps.
  • Genital and anal skin lesions need location-specific treatment.
  • A painless or familiar-looking lump can still need assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Does a hard anal lump mean cancer?

No. Clotted haemorrhoids, skin conditions and other non-cancerous problems are common possibilities. A new or persistent lump still needs an examination because its feel alone cannot identify the cause.

When should I seek urgent help?

Seek emergency help for heavy or ongoing bleeding or severe pain. Fever with worsening anal pain, spreading redness or pus needs prompt assessment. A retained rectal object also needs urgent medical help.

Can a painless lump be ignored?

No. Warts, skin tags and other benign changes can be painless, but pain is not a reliable test for seriousness. Have a new, growing, bleeding or persistent lump checked.

Can rubber bands treat an external haemorrhoid?

Rubber-band ligation is for appropriate internal haemorrhoids. It is not a home treatment and is not used to band an external lump. A clinician should confirm the type before discussing a procedure.

Should I drain a blue-purple lump myself?

No. A clot, abscess or another lesion can be injured or infected by attempts to puncture it. Seek assessment, particularly if it is severely painful or growing.

Is hidradenitis caused by poor hygiene?

No. HS is an inflammatory condition involving hair follicles, not a sign of being unclean. Recurrent painful nodules, scarring and drainage deserve an individual treatment plan.

Are anal warts and molluscum the same?

No. Different viruses cause them and their treatments differ. Both can resemble other skin changes, so a clinician should identify an anal or genital lesion before treatment.

Is imiquimod the standard treatment for every molluscum bump?

No. Treatment depends on age, location and health. Many lesions resolve, but genital or anal lesions should be assessed. CDC does not recommend imiquimod for molluscum in children.

Will constipation treatment remove every anal lump?

No. Easier bowel movements may reduce straining and pressure, but a separate skin growth, clot or infection may need different care. Persistent symptoms require reassessment.

Will I need a colonoscopy?

Not necessarily. Inspection and an anal examination may establish the cause. Further tests depend on bleeding, bowel changes, examination findings, age and individual risk.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
